overview.title: Doctor Strange, decade by decade
overview.lede: Doctor Strange began as five pages at the back of a Human Torch comic, with no cover billing and no expectation of lasting, and became the strangest-looking thing Marvel published. The reason is mostly one man: Steve Ditko had no room for fight choreography in a five-page strip, so he drew rooms instead — folded staircases, floating rock, planes of colour with no horizon — and invented what a magic dimension looks like in comics. Everything since is people deciding what to do with a character whose visual language arrived before his personality did.

sections.h: Ditko, and the five pages that invented a visual language
body: Strange Tales #110, July 1963. The Doctor Strange strip runs at the back of a Human Torch book, five pages an issue, and for the first several issues he has no origin, no explanation and no cover billing — he is simply a man in a New York townhouse whom frightened people come to see.

The origin does not arrive until #115, and it is worth knowing how unusual it is: a brilliant, arrogant surgeon wrecks his hands in a car crash, refuses every job beneath him, drinks himself down to the docks, and goes to Tibet to be cured. He is not cured. He is given something else instead. No other Marvel hero of the period starts as a failure who does not get what he came for.

The page count is what makes the art. Ditko has no space for a fight, so he spends it on architecture that could not exist — and because nobody had drawn a magic dimension before, there was no house style to argue with. Look at how little rendering there is: flat colour, hard contour, and shapes that read as impossible purely because of how they connect.

By #138 Ditko is writing the strip as well as drawing it, and that is when Eternity appears — the universe itself drawn as a man-shaped silhouette full of stars, which remains the single best-known image the character has produced. He left after #146.

fig.cap: Left: Strange Tales #110 — note whose book this is; Doctor Strange is not on the cover. Right: #138, the Eternity issue, written and drawn by Ditko.

makers.b: Look at the negative space. Ditko builds a dimension by drawing a few hard-edged objects and then leaving the rest of the panel empty or flat-coloured — no atmosphere, no gradient, no rendering. The eeriness comes from what he refuses to draw.

The oaths. The Vishanti, the Crimson Bands of Cyttorak, the Hoary Hosts of Hoggoth. Lee never explains any of them, which is exactly why they work — they sound like a real liturgy overheard rather than a magic system being described.

sections.h: Losing Ditko, and the costume nobody defends
body: Ditko walks, and the strip has to work out what it is without the only person who had ever drawn it. Bill Everett, then Marie Severin, then Gene Colan — and Colan is the one who sticks, because he takes it somewhere Ditko never did: soft, fleshy, smoke and half-light, with a Strange who has visible weight and worry.

Strange Tales ends at #168 and the Doctor Strange half takes the numbering with it — Doctor Strange #169 is the next issue, and the Nick Fury half becomes its own book. So the two halves of the second omnibus are one continuous run, not two.

Then the decision everyone remembers: in #177 he gets a full-face mask and a costume, on the theory that he was not enough of a superhero. It is almost universally regarded as a mistake, and it is genuinely worth seeing — partly because Colan draws it beautifully anyway, and partly because it is the clearest evidence of the pressure the book was under.
It did not save it. Cancelled at #183 in 1969. The character survives the next two years as a guest in other people's comics.

fig.cap: Left: #169 — his own title at last, continuing Strange Tales' numbering. Right: #177, the mask.

makers.b: Look at the edges. Colan barely uses a hard contour line — forms emerge out of tone and shadow, which is why his Strange looks like he is standing in actual air. It is the opposite of Ditko's approach and it is the other great answer to how this book should look.

sections.h: The non-team, and the strangest book Marvel printed in the seventies
body: With no title of his own, Strange does the thing he is best at: he assembles people who do not want to be assembled. Marvel Feature #1 is the last thing printed in his own omnibus and the first thing in the Defenders' — he calls the Hulk and the Sub-Mariner, and the non-team exists.

The joke of the Defenders is that it is an Avengers comic with no mansion, no butler, no charter and nobody who likes anybody. Strange is the only member who wants the group to exist, which gives him a function no other book gave him: he is the responsible adult in a room of people who resent him.

The Avengers/Defenders War in 1973 is the first great hero-versus-hero crossover and still one of the best-structured — pairs of heroes fight over fragments of the Evil Eye while both teams are being played by Loki and Dormammu.

Then Steve Gerber takes over and the book becomes something else entirely. The Headmen, four scientists who have each done something irreversible to their own skulls. Bambi and the Bozos. And the Elf With a Gun, who turns up at random, murders a stranger, and is never explained — because Gerber thought a universe that always explains itself is a lie. It is funny and then abruptly not.

fig.cap: Left: Marvel Feature #1 — the hand-off between two omnibuses on this shelf. Right: Defenders #31, mid-Gerber.

makers.b: Watch what he does with tone breaks. A Gerber issue will run a genuinely silly premise straight-faced for fifteen pages and then land something bleak in the last two, with no change in register. The Elf is the purest version: a running gag that is also a murder.
The plainness is the point. Buscema draws Gerber's absurdities with completely straight, sturdy, unglamorous storytelling, and that deadpan is what makes them funny instead of arch.

sections.h: Englehart and Brunner: the best-drawn the book has ever been
body: He gets a solo strip back in Marvel Premiere in 1972, and the first half is a scramble — Barry Windsor-Smith draws #3–4, then Gardner Fox scripts a stretch drawn by, among others, P. Craig Russell and a young Jim Starlin. Four remarkable artists in six issues and no settled direction.

Then Steve Englehart and Frank Brunner arrive at #9 and it becomes the run people mean when they say Doctor Strange is the best-drawn book Marvel ever had. Brunner comes off underground comix and draws Strange as Art Nouveau — whiplash contour, deep blacks, decorative borders, and faces that actually look frightened.

The Sise-Neg saga in Marvel Premiere #12–14 sends Strange backwards through the whole of human history to the moment of creation, where a sorcerer accumulating power across time arrives at the beginning and becomes God. Marvel's own Comics Code office objected for precisely the reason you would guess, and Englehart and Brunner reportedly forged a letter of complaint to force the issue through.
Gene Colan returns at #6 of the 1974 series and stays for years. The omnibus stops at #22 of a run that goes to #81, which is where the shelf's first real hole opens.

fig.cap: Left: Marvel Premiere #14, the end of Sise-Neg. Right: the 1974 #1 — Brunner's border work is the thing to look at.

makers.b: Look at the panel borders. Brunner treats the frame as decoration — borders that curl, dissolve, or become part of the spell being cast. Almost nobody at Marvel was doing that in 1973, and it comes straight out of underground comix and Art Nouveau posters.

He writes cosmology as plot. Most magic comics use the mystical as set dressing; Englehart builds stories whose actual stakes are metaphysical — who made the universe, and what happens if the answer is disappointing.

sections.h: The missing decade: Stern, Rogers, and no omnibus at all
body: This stretch is not on the shelf and it is Marvel's doing, not a curation call. Doctor Strange (1974) #23–81 has never been collected in omnibus — Epic Collections and Masterworks only.

What is in it matters. Roger Stern wrote the back half of that run and Marshall Rogers drew a celebrated stretch of it, including the much-reprinted #55; the run also contains the Dracula story that got Marvel into trouble with the Code, and the introduction of a lot of the modern furniture of the character.
So the shelf jumps from 1977 to 1988 with a decade missing in the middle. The note on the Master of the Mystic Arts tile says so.

fig.cap: Doctor Strange #55, Stern and Rogers — uncollected in omnibus, and one of the best-regarded issues the title has.

sections.h: Sorcerer Supreme: ninety issues of treating it as a job
body: After a year with no book, the 1988 relaunch opens by taking everything off him — the Sanctum burned, the library gone, the title of Sorcerer Supreme genuinely in question. Peter B. Gillis writes the rebuild; Roy Thomas takes over at #5 and settles the book into the shape it keeps for ninety issues.

That shape is unusual and is the reason this run has a following: it is an occult procedural. The magic has rules, costs, precedent and paperwork, and Thomas — a genuine Marvel historian — treats sixty years of continuity as a case file. It is the least flashy era on this shelf and the one most interested in the job of being Sorcerer Supreme.

In 1992 Marvel builds a horror line around him. Rise of the Midnight Sons runs through six titles at once, and once again Strange's function is convening people — Ghost Rider, Morbius, the Nightstalkers, the Darkhold Redeemers. Secret Defenders is the same idea done better: a different roster every arc, hand-picked by Strange for the specific job, none of them told why.

The last thirty issues get strange in the other sense. David Quinn has Strange lose his powers and start drawing on something called the Vapors; Warren Ellis arrives around #80 for a short, cold stretch; J.M. DeMatteis closes it out in 1996, and the character has no ongoing title for nineteen years.

fig.cap: Left: the 1988 relaunch #1. Right: #50 — Geof Isherwood, mid-Midnight Sons.

makers.b: Watch how often a story turns on a rule rather than a punch — a prior bargain, an obligation, a precedent from a comic published twenty years earlier. Thomas is the reason this run reads as a professional practice with a history.
The texture. Buckingham's back-half issues are the best-looking thing in the last third of this run — dense linework and a real feel for decorative pattern, well before Fables made him famous.

sections.h: Nineteen years, one great book, and no omnibus for any of it
body: This is the largest hole on the shelf. Between the end of Sorcerer Supreme in 1996 and the 2015 relaunch there is no omnibus at all, and the gap contains the single best-regarded Doctor Strange story of the last thirty years.

The Oath (2006), by Brian K. Vaughan and Marcos Martin, is a five-issue detective story: Strange is shot, and the investigation turns into an argument about whether a man who can cure anything is obliged to. Martin's cartooning on it — clean, geometric, formally inventive page architecture — is routinely cited as some of the best storytelling of its decade.

Also in the gap: J. Michael Straczynski and Brandon Peterson's Strange (2004), and the whole of the Bendis-era Avengers material where Strange spends years as a supporting character in other people's books.
None of it is collected in this format. The note on the Aaron and Bachalo tile says so.

fig.cap: The Oath #1, 2006. The best-reviewed Doctor Strange story there is, and it has no omnibus.

sections.h: Aaron and Bachalo: magic has a bill and somebody is paying it
body: The first ongoing in nineteen years, and it has one strong idea: every spell costs something, and the cost does not vanish because you stopped looking at it. Aaron's Strange eats things that are still moving, keeps a cellar full of obligations, and is quietly in enormous debt.

That turns the character from a man with answers into a man with bills, which is the most useful reframing anyone has done with him since Ditko. Then the Empirikul arrive — a crusade dedicated to burning magic out of the universe entirely — and the back half is Strange with nothing, which is where the run gets good.

Chris Bachalo draws it with the density turned all the way up: panels crammed with talking objects, impossible interiors, and a Sanctum that is clearly alive and clearly listening. It is divisive — the recurring criticism is that the storytelling can be hard to follow — and it is unmistakably its own thing.

fig.cap: Left: the 2015 #1. Right: #6 — the Empirikul arc, and Bachalo at full density.

makers.b: Look at the backgrounds, not the figures. Bachalo fills every corner of the Sanctum with small objects that are watching, muttering, or eating — the room does the characterisation. Then notice how empty the pages go once the Empirikul have won.

sections.h: MacKay kills him, and hands the book to Clea
body: The Death of Doctor Strange opens on his corpse, which sounds like a stunt and is actually the setup for a properly constructed murder mystery: a younger Strange, summoned from the past, gets a limited window to investigate his own death. The clues are fairly played and the solution is earned.

Then the genuinely good decision. Strange stays dead for a while and the book goes to Clea — Dormammu's niece, his former student and wife, a character who spent fifty years being a rescue object — who becomes Sorcerer Supreme of Earth and is better at it and much less nice about it. Jed MacKay writes ten issues of her trying to bring him back that are the best Clea material anyone has written.
The 2023 ongoing puts them both in the Sanctum as a married couple running a practice together, which is a premise no previous era would have reached for and which works.

fig.cap: Left: The Death of Doctor Strange #1. Right: Strange #1 — Clea's book.

makers.b: Notice how tightly plotted it is for a book about magic. MacKay sets rules in issue one and then refuses to break them for convenience, which is rare in this corner of Marvel and is why the mystery works.

tone.sub: Ten volumes that disagree about whether this is a horror strip, a cosmology, a sitcom about a bad team, or a procedural.

modes.b: Ditko's five-page backups. Impossible architecture drawn flat and hard, and the moment the universe turns out to be a man-shaped hole full of stars.
Englehart and Brunner, then Colan. Art Nouveau borders, deep blacks, and a story that goes back to the moment of creation and finds somebody already there.
Gerber's Defenders. The Headmen, Bambi and the Bozos, and an elf who shoots a stranger for no reason anyone ever explains.
The non-team's first five years, including the Avengers/Defenders War — the first great hero-versus-hero crossover.
Sorcerer Supreme. Ninety issues of rules, costs, precedent and paperwork, with Roy Thomas treating sixty years of continuity as a case file.
The end of Sorcerer Supreme — Strange loses his powers and starts drawing on the Vapors, a bargain readers have argued about for thirty years.
Aaron and Bachalo. Magic has a price, Strange is in debt for all of it, and then someone burns magic out of the world.
MacKay. A murder mystery where the detective is the victim, and then ten issues of Clea being better at his job than he was.

ds-o1.title: Doctor Strange Omnibus Vol. 1
ds-o1.lede: Thirty-five five-page backup strips that invented what magic looks like in comics, and one Spider-Man annual.

sections.h: Five pages at the back of somebody else's comic
body: The format is the whole story. Doctor Strange runs at the back of Strange Tales, behind the Human Torch, at five pages an issue, with no cover billing for years. Ditko has no room for a fight, so he draws the place instead.

For the first four instalments there is no origin at all — he is simply a man in a Greenwich Village townhouse whom frightened people visit. #115 finally explains him, and the explanation is unusual: an arrogant surgeon ruins his hands, refuses honest work, drinks his way down, goes to Tibet to be healed and is not. He gets a vocation instead of a cure.
The run builds to the Eternity saga across #130–146 — a chase through realities against Dormammu and Mordo that ends with Strange meeting the universe itself. By that point Ditko is writing it too.
Note the strip skipped Strange Tales #112–113, so the book does. The one non-Strange Tales item is Amazing Spider-Man Annual #2, an early crossover.

fig.cap: #115 — “The Origin of Dr. Strange”, and a hero who does not get what he went for.

makers.b: Count the textures. There are almost none. Ditko renders nothing: flat colour, hard contour, and impossible geometry that reads as impossible purely from how the shapes connect to each other.

verdict.standing: The foundation, and still the strangest-looking
body: Widely held to be one of the two or three most influential visual runs of the Silver Age, and the reason the character exists in the form he does. The Eternity sequence in particular is reproduced constantly well outside comics.

The honest caveat is the format: these are five-page instalments, and read thirty-five in a row they are repetitive in structure — a threat, a journey, an incantation, a resolution. Readers who bounce off it usually bounce off that, not off the art.

ds-o2.title: Doctor Strange Omnibus Vol. 2
ds-o2.lede: Ditko leaves, Colan arrives, the strip graduates to its own title, and it is cancelled inside two years.

sections.h: One continuous run, printed in two halves
body: The important structural fact: Strange Tales ends at #168 and Doctor Strange #169 picks the numbering straight up. The Nick Fury half of the split book became its own title at the same time. So this omnibus is one continuous run even though it looks like two series.

Artistically it is a search. Bill Everett follows Ditko, then Marie Severin takes a long stretch, and then Gene Colan arrives and defines the book's second look — tonal, smoky, figures emerging out of shadow rather than being contained by outline.

#177 puts him in a full-face mask. It is the single most criticised design decision in the character's history and it is instructive: the book was being pushed to look more like a superhero comic, and looking like a superhero comic is precisely what it could not do.

Cancelled at #183. The volume closes with the guest appearances that kept him alive and then Marvel Feature #1, where he founds the Defenders — which is the first thing in the next book on this shelf.

fig.cap: #177 — the mask. Colan draws it beautifully and it was still a mistake.

makers.b: One of very few women drawing mainstream Marvel in the sixties, and the transitional artist who kept the strip coherent between Ditko and Colan. Look at her page compositions — much more classically balanced than either of them.

verdict.standing: A transitional book, and the mask is genuinely divisive
body: Readers split on this era. The case for it is Colan, who is one of the great Marvel artists and who gives the character a physical presence Ditko never aimed for. The case against is that the writing drifts, chasing a superhero register that does not suit the strip — and the costume is the emblem of that.
Almost everyone agrees the ending is a real loss: the book was getting better as it was cancelled.

def-o1.title: Defenders Omnibus Vol. 1
def-o1.lede: Strange calls the two most antisocial people he knows and accidentally runs a team for five years.

sections.h: A team book for people who hate team books
body: It opens on Marvel Feature #1, the issue the previous omnibus closes on, so these two books hand off to each other cleanly — the only shared issue on this shelf.

The premise is a genuine innovation: no charter, no headquarters, no roster and no affection. The Hulk does not want to be there, Namor is contemptuous of everyone, and Strange is the only one who thinks the group should exist. That gives him the role his solo books never found — the one adult, permanently negotiating.

The Avengers/Defenders War is the centrepiece and it is still a model of how to build a crossover: the two teams are pointed at each other by Loki and Dormammu, the fights are paired off so each is a real matchup, and the misunderstanding is resolved without either side looking stupid.

One warning about how it is printed. The four Avengers issues are collected as a block at the end rather than interleaved with Defenders #8–11, which is how Marvel's own collecting line lists them too — so read the two halves together rather than in the order the pages fall.

fig.cap: Left: Defenders #1. Right: Avengers #116 — printed at the back of this book, but read it in sequence.

verdict.standing: A classic, and the crossover holds up
body: The early Defenders is well regarded and the Avengers/Defenders War is consistently named among the best crossovers of the era — largely because it is short, structurally clean, and has an actual reason for the fight.

The recurring criticism is that the first stretch under Roy Thomas is conventional monster-of-the-month material and takes a while to find the tone the book becomes famous for. That tone arrives in the next volume.

def-o2.title: Defenders Omnibus Vol. 2
def-o2.lede: Steve Gerber's run, and the strangest superhero comic Marvel published in the seventies.

sections.h: The Headmen, the Bozos, and an elf with a gun
body: Gerber uses the non-team as somewhere to put ideas that fit nowhere else, and the results are genuinely unlike anything around them. The Headmen are four scientists who have each done something irreversible to their own skulls. Bambi and the Bozos are a satire of self-help cults that turns nasty. And the Elf With a Gun appears at random, kills a bystander, and is never explained.

That last one is the key to the run. Gerber's position was that a fictional universe which always eventually explains itself is dishonest about how the world works, so the Elf is a deliberate unresolved wound in the book.

Strange is mostly the straight man here, and it is the most interesting he has ever been in a team book — the register of a serious occultist reacting to genuine nonsense does more for the character than a hundred incantations.

The three 1950s and 1960s horror shorts at the back — Mystery Tales #21, World of Fantasy #11, Tales of Suspense #9 — are backmatter reprints tied to the Headmen, which is why this volume's dates run much wider than its run does.

fig.cap: Defenders #31 — Sal Buscema playing it completely straight, which is what makes it work.

makers.b: Read the captions. Gerber narrates in a dry, essayistic voice that keeps commenting on the story from just outside it — and that gap between the voice and the events is where the whole run lives.

verdict.standing: A cult classic, and the most argued-about book on this shelf
body: Gerber's Defenders has an enormous reputation among writers — it is cited constantly as an influence by people who came up in the eighties and nineties — and it is one of the first mainstream superhero runs that is obviously authored rather than produced.

It is also the one readers most often bounce off. The recurring criticism is that it is wilfully shapeless, that the jokes date badly, and that the Elf is either the bravest thing in seventies Marvel or a gag that never lands, depending on who you ask. Both readings are common and both are defensible.

mystic-o1.title: Doctor Strange: Master of the Mystic Arts Omnibus
mystic-o1.lede: Four extraordinary artists in six issues, then Englehart and Brunner, then Colan for years.

sections.h: The scramble, then the run
body: Marvel Premiere #3–8 is a remarkable mess: Barry Windsor-Smith draws the first two, then Gardner Fox scripts a stretch drawn by, among others, P. Craig Russell and a very young Jim Starlin. Four major artists, no settled direction, six issues.

Englehart and Brunner arrive at #9 and the book locks in. Brunner's Strange is Art Nouveau — whiplash line, decorative borders, heavy blacks — and he treats the panel frame itself as something a spell can act on.

The Sise-Neg saga, #12–14, is the centrepiece: Strange travels backwards through human history to the instant of creation, pursuing a sorcerer who is absorbing magic from every era he passes and who arrives at the beginning with enough power to be the one who starts it. The Comics Code objected.

sections.h: His own title again, and Colan settles in
body: The 1974 series opens with Englehart and Brunner, and then Gene Colan takes over at #6 and stays. This is the second long Colan stretch on the character and the one most people mean — tonal, atmospheric, and completely unlike the hard-edged Ditko tradition.

The book runs to #81 in 1987. This omnibus stops at #22, which means Roger Stern and Marshall Rogers's celebrated later run is not here and is not collected in omnibus anywhere. That is the shelf's first real hole.

fig.cap: Marvel Premiere #3 — Barry Windsor-Smith, and the strip's return after three years as a guest.

sections.shelfLabel: The other side of the gap

verdict.standing: Widely held to be the best-drawn era the character has had
body: The Englehart and Brunner stretch is the one most often named when people argue for Doctor Strange as a great comic rather than a great design, and the Sise-Neg saga has a reputation well beyond the character's own readership.
The criticism, such as it is, concerns pacing: Englehart's metaphysics can stall, and the 1974 series loses momentum in its second half as the creative team turns over. Nobody argues about the art.

sss-o1.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus Vol. 1
sss-o1.lede: A relaunch that starts by taking everything away, then settles into an occult procedural.

sections.h: Rebuilt from nothing, then given a job
body: The 1988 #1 opens with the Sanctum burned, the library destroyed, his allies scattered and the title of Sorcerer Supreme genuinely in dispute. Peter B. Gillis writes that rebuild.

From #5 Roy Thomas takes over and gives the book the identity it keeps for ninety issues: an occult procedural, where magic has rules, prices and precedent, and where Thomas's encyclopedic command of Marvel history means a twenty-year-old bargain can be the thing a story turns on.
Jackson Guice pencils the early run in a clean, controlled late-eighties style — the least mannered art on this shelf, and deliberately so. This is a book about competence.
One Ghost Rider issue is here, which is the first hint of the horror line Marvel is about to build around him.

fig.cap: The 1988 relaunch #1 — everything taken away in the first issue.

verdict.standing: Undervalued, and the most consistent run on the shelf
body: This era has a quiet, durable following. The case for it is that it is the only long stretch that takes the job seriously — the reader comes away understanding what being Sorcerer Supreme actually involves, which is not true of the flashier runs.

The recurring criticism is that it is visually plain next to Ditko, Brunner or Bachalo, and that Thomas's continuity density can read as homework. Readers who want the strip to look strange find it conventional.

sss-o2.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus Vol. 2
sss-o2.lede: Marvel builds a horror line around him, and Secret Defenders lets him assemble a new team every arc.

sections.h: Midnight Sons, and the best use of the character's actual talent
body: Rise of the Midnight Sons runs through six titles at once in 1992, and once again Strange's function is convening people — Ghost Rider, Morbius, the Nightstalkers, the Darkhold Redeemers. The Ghost Rider, Morbius and Silver Surfer chapters printed here are the same crossover the Ghost Rider shelf reads from the other side.

Secret Defenders is the same idea done better, and it is the reason to own this volume. Strange picks a different roster for every arc, chosen for the specific job, and does not tell them why they were chosen. It is a genuinely good format and it uses the one thing this character is better at than anyone else in Marvel.

Geof Isherwood draws most of it and eventually writes it as well. It is the most 1990s material on the shelf and it wears that plainly — heavy rendering, crossover architecture, a lot of covers with skulls on.

verdict.standing: Divisive, and Secret Defenders is better than its reputation
body: The Midnight Sons material is very much of its moment and readers who dislike 1990s Marvel dislike this on sight — the crossover obligations do interrupt the book repeatedly, which is the fair version of the complaint.
Secret Defenders, though, is regularly singled out as an underrated format, and it is the strongest argument on this shelf that Doctor Strange works best as a man who assembles other people.

sss-o3.title: Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme Omnibus Vol. 3
sss-o3.lede: The last thirty issues, in which he loses his powers and starts drawing on something called the Vapors.

sections.h: Quinn, then Ellis, then the end
body: David Quinn writes the bulk of this book, from #60 into the high seventies, and takes it somewhere genuinely strange: Strange loses his powers and begins drawing on a substance called the Vapors, a bargain with an unmistakable cost. Readers have argued about it for thirty years and it is, at minimum, unlike anything else in the character's history.

Warren Ellis arrives around #80 for a short, cold stretch that strips the mysticism back to something more clinical — recognisably early Ellis, and worth the price of admission on its own. J.M. DeMatteis closes the run out in 1996.
Mark Buckingham draws a lot of the back half and is the best reason to look at it, well before Fables made him a name.

The tail of the volume is the loose material: an ashcan, a magazine chapter, Kurt Busiek's 1994 Strange Tales one-shot, and What Is It That Disturbs You, Stephen?, a 1997 painted graphic novel — which is why the dates run past the run's own end.
After this the character has no ongoing title for nineteen years.

fig.cap: What comes next, and is not on this shelf: The Oath, 2006.

sections.shelfLabel: The other side of the gap

verdict.standing: The low point for some readers, a cult favourite for others
body: The Vapors storyline is the most divisive thing on this shelf. The criticism is that it is a 1990s edginess exercise that fundamentally misreads the character — a sorcerer defined by discipline turned into an addict — and that the art through the middle stretch is inconsistent.

The defence is that it is the only time anyone let this book be genuinely unpleasant, and that the Ellis and Buckingham issues near the end are as good as anything in the ninety-issue run. Go in knowing it is contested.

aaron-o1.title: Doctor Strange by Aaron & Bachalo Omnibus
aaron-o1.lede: Magic costs something, Strange has been running a tab for years, and then someone burns magic out of the world.

sections.h: The bill arrives
body: The first ongoing in nineteen years, and its central idea is the best reframing of the character since Ditko: every spell has a price, and Strange has been deferring his. He eats things that are still moving, keeps a cellar of obligations, and is quietly, enormously in debt.

That converts him from a man with answers into a man with liabilities, which is immediately more interesting to read. Then the Empirikul arrive — a crusade dedicated to eradicating magic from the universe — and win. The back half is Strange with no power, no library and no tools, which is where the run earns its reputation.

Chris Bachalo draws it at maximum density: interiors crowded with small objects that watch and mutter, a Sanctum that is clearly alive, and colour he does himself. Then, once the Empirikul have won, the pages go conspicuously empty.

fig.cap: #6 — the Empirikul arc. Look at what is happening in the backgrounds.

verdict.standing: Well regarded, and the art is the argument
body: The premise is very widely praised — “magic has a cost” is the idea most often credited with making the character legible to modern readers, and it arrived alongside the film that did the same commercially.

Bachalo is the split. Admirers consider him one of the most inventive designers in mainstream comics; the recurring criticism is that his page architecture can be genuinely hard to follow, with the eye losing the reading order. It is a real complaint, not a taste dispute, and how much it costs you decides how much you like this book.

mackay-o1.title: Doctor Strange by Jed MacKay Omnibus
mackay-o1.lede: A murder mystery where the detective is the victim, and then the best Clea story anyone has written.

sections.h: Kill him in issue one
body: The Death of Doctor Strange opens on the body and then does something properly clever: a younger Strange is summoned from the past with a limited window to solve his own murder. It is a fairly played mystery — the clues are on the page — which is rare for a book about magic.

Then the run's real decision. Strange stays dead, and the book goes to Clea — Dormammu's niece, his student, his wife, and for fifty years mostly a person things happened to. She becomes Sorcerer Supreme of Earth and is better at it and considerably less nice about it, and MacKay writes ten issues of her working to bring him back.

The 2023 ongoing lands them both in the Sanctum as a married couple running a practice together — a domestic premise no earlier era would have tried, and it works because MacKay has spent thirty issues earning it.

fig.cap: The 2023 ongoing — both of them, in the Sanctum, working.

verdict.standing: The best-reviewed modern run, and Clea is the reason
body: Reception has been strong and unusually consistent: the mystery is praised for actually being a mystery, and the Strange series with Clea in the lead is frequently named the best thing done with that character in her entire existence.

The mild criticism is that it is conventional next to the shelf's stranger corners — competent, tightly plotted superhero comics rather than the formal adventure of Ditko, Brunner or Bachalo. If what you want from this character is strangeness, this is the least strange book here.
